title: Usages of Keras Augmentaiton Layers
body: I was trying to use RandomRotation in a custom class based setup with tf.data API. ```python class RandRotateKeras3D: def __init__(self, keys, factor=0.1, prob=0.8, fill_value=0.0): self.keys = keys self.prob = prob self.fill_value = fill_value self.seed_val = np.random.randint(0, 10**6) self.img_rotate = layers.RandomRotation( factor=factor, fill_mode="constant", interpolation="bilinear", fill_value=fill_value, seed=self.seed_val ) self.label_rotate = layers.RandomRotation( factor=factor, fill_mode="constant", interpolation="nearest", fill_value=0.0, seed=self.seed_val ) def __call__(self, inputs): image_key, label_key = self.keys img = inputs.data[image_key] lbl = inputs.data[label_key] img_shape = tf.shape(img) D, H, W = img_shape[0], img_shape[1], img_shape[2] # Padding pad_h, pad_w = H // 2, W // 2 img_padded = tf.pad( img, [[0, 0], [pad_h, pad_h], [pad_w, pad_w], [0, 0]], constant_values=tf.cast(self.fill_value, img.dtype) ) lbl_padded = tf.pad( lbl, [[0, 0], [pad_h, pad_h], [pad_w, pad_w], [0, 0]], constant_values=tf.cast(0, lbl.dtype) ) # Transpose to (Batch=1, H, W, Channels=D) img_trans = tf.transpose(img_padded, [3, 1, 2, 0]) lbl_trans = tf.transpose(lbl_padded, [3, 1, 2, 0]) img_rot = self.img_rotate(img_trans) lbl_rot = self.label_rotate(lbl_trans) # Transpose back and crop img_final = tf.transpose(img_rot, [3, 1, 2, 0]) lbl_final = tf.transpose(lbl_rot, [3, 1, 2, 0]) img_final = tf.image.resize_with_crop_or_pad(img_final, H, W) lbl_final = tf.image.resize_with_crop_or_pad(lbl_final, H, W) return ... ``` I got ```bash ValueError: in user code: File "/tmp/ipykernel_47/2758838664.py", line 48, in train_transformation * result = pipeline(data) File "/usr/local/lib/python3.11/dist-packages/medicai/transforms/base.py", line 53, in __call__ * x = transform(x) File "/tmp/ipykernel_47/285916447.py", line 138, in __call__ * img_rot = self.img_rotate(img_trans) File "/usr/local/lib/python3.11/dist-packages/keras/src/layers/preprocessing/data_layer.py", line 119, in __call__ ** outputs = super().__call__(inputs, **kwargs) File "/usr/local/lib/python3.11/dist-packages/keras/src/utils/traceback_utils.py", line 122, in error_handler raise e.with_traceback(filtered_tb) from None ValueError: Exception encountered when calling RandomRotation.call(). tf.function only supports singleton tf.Variables created on the first call. Make sure the tf.Variable is only created once or created outside tf.function. See https:///guide/function#creating_tfvariables for more information. Arguments received by RandomRotation.call(): • data= • training=True ``` ## Queries 1. In the setup described above, is it considered invalid or discouraged to instantiate random augmentation layers once and invoke them inside the call method, particularly when used within a `tf.data` pipeline or `tf.function`? I tested the code outside the tf.data and it works well. Furthermore, while checking out the output, I noticed that, due to rotation, some border effect was obvious. To remedy that, would it be nice to add `cropping` after the rotation, i.e. see the following output (`A` is not desired but `B`) - taken from [here](https://github.com/kobiso/Image-Rotation-and-Cropping-tensorflow/tree/master). 2. I aimed to implement a custom random-rotation layer. However, at present, there is no equivalent operation in Keras 3 to `tfa.image.rotate`. It would be highly beneficial if such a stateless, low-level rotation primitive were available natively in Keras 3. Hopefully, it will behave nicely in tf.data API regardless of the backend. 3. Regarding the existing [Keras image augmentation layers](https://keras.io/api/layers/preprocessing_layers/image_augmentation/): - These layers do not expose a probability (**prob**) argument to explicitly control whether a random transformation is applied. What is the motivation behind omitting such a parameter, given that probabilistic control is closely tied to augmentation behavior and is important for analyzing experimental impact? I thought it was added in `keras-cv` with `rate` flag, not sure if it is still true. - The current API is designed to operate on a single input tensor, which is appropriate for image classification. However, for segmentation tasks, how is one expected to reliably ensure that identical random transformations are applied to both the input image and its corresponding label or mask? Additionally, since labels are discrete, even minor geometric distortions can introduce spatial noise—how is this concern intended to be addressed within the current design? - Lastly, the official documentation for several Keras augmentation layers does not provide concrete code examples. For instance, layers such as [RandomShear](https://keras.io/api/layers/preprocessing_layers/image_augmentation/random_shear/) and [RandomTranslation](https://keras.io/api/layers/preprocessing_layers/image_augmentation/random_translation/) are described only at the API level, without minimal, runnable examples demonstrating their usage, inputs, and expected outputs. This makes the behavior of these layers unintuitive to understand. Including simple, illustrative examples would significantly improve usability, user engagement, and confidence in these APIs.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
@reporter 

1.
    a. I believe this is simply because you're overriding `__call__` instead of `call`, which leads to weird errors. Do `def call(self, inputs):` instead.

    b. That is a gap indeed. We could augment the API by adding `fill_mode="crop"`.

2. You can use [`keras.ops.image.affine_transform`](https://keras.io/api/ops/image/#affinetransform-function). The missing part is that you have to create the affine transform matrix. The code is here: https://github.com/keras-team/keras/blob/master/keras/src/layers/preprocessing/image_preprocessing/base_image_preprocessing_layer.py#L320-L337

3.
    a. Well it's not a question whether the transform is applied or not, the whole point is that you always apply some rotation so that the training never sees the same image again. The control you have is the `factor` argument of `RandomRotation` which controls how much you rotate at most. Then, for each image a random angle is picked and applied.

    b. You're supposed to pass the following structure (any of `"bounding_boxes"`, `"labels"`, `"segmentation_masks"` can be missing):
    ```
    {
      "images": images,
      "bounding_boxes": bounding_boxes,
      "labels": labels,
      "segmentation_masks": segmentation_masks,
    } 
    ```
    Then everything is rotated the same way. The truth is that this may not be documented.

    c. It does look like there isn't a thorough example for this indeed. Were you thinking in the docstring of the API or as an example on keras.io?

comments.body: Hi @reporter, I've implemented `fill_mode="crop"` for `keras.layers.RandomRotation` and would like your feedback on the approach before finalizing. **Key idea** - For `fill_mode="crop"`, the layer: 1. Pads the input to the diagonal size (`ceil(sqrt(H^2 + W^2))`) so any rotation fits. 2. Applies the rotation on the padded canvas with `fill_mode="constant", fill_value=0.0`. 3. Applies a conservative center crop (`~1/sqrt(2)` of original H,W) that is guaranteed to remove all border/canvas artifacts for any rotation angle, while staying backend‑friendly and batched. This is less aggressive than full angle‑dependent LRR math, but guarantees that the cropped region contains **no fill pixels**, which matches your "cropped out should not contain fill value" requirement. **Visual result** (using Colab demo script): **Code sketch** ``` def _apply_rotation_with_crop(self, images, transformation, interpolation): orig_h = transformation["image_height"] orig_w = transformation["image_width"] padded = self._pad_for_crop(images, orig_h, orig_w) padded_h, padded_w = self._get_hw(padded) padded_rotation_matrix = self._compute_affine_matrix( center_x=0.5, center_y=0.5, angle=transformation["angle"], translate_x=ops.numpy.zeros([transformation["batch_size"]]), translate_y=ops.numpy.zeros([transformation["batch_size"]]), scale=ops.numpy.ones([transformation["batch_size"]]), shear_x=ops.numpy.zeros([transformation["batch_size"]]), shear_y=ops.numpy.zeros([transformation["batch_size"]]), height=padded_h, width=padded_w, ) rotated = self._apply_affine( images=padded, rotation_matrix=padded_rotation_matrix, interpolation=interpolation, fill_mode="constant", fill_value=0.0, ) return self._conservative_inner_crop(rotated, orig_h, orig_w) def _conservative_inner_crop(self, images, orig_h, orig_w): factor = ops.cast(0.70710678, "float32") orig_h = ops.cast(orig_h, "float32") orig_w = ops.cast(orig_w, "float32") crop_h = ops.cast(orig_h * factor, "int32") crop_w = ops.cast(orig_w * factor, "int32") shape = ops.shape(images) if self.data_format == "channels_last": curr_h = shape[1] curr_w = shape[2] channels = shape[3] offset_h = (curr_h - crop_h) // 2 offset_w = (curr_w - crop_w) // 2 cropped = ops.slice( images, start_indices=[0, offset_h, offset_w, 0], shape=[shape[0], crop_h, crop_w, channels], ) else: curr_h = shape[2] curr_w = shape[3] channels = shape[1] offset_h = (curr_h - crop_h) // 2 offset_w = (curr_w - crop_w) // 2 cropped = ops.slice( images, start_indices=[0, 0, offset_h, offset_w], shape=[shape[0], channels, crop_h, crop_w], ) return cropped ```

comments.body:
Thanks for the questions @participant6 and @reporter !

To clarify the current implementation in the PR:

- `fill_mode="crop"` does **not** shrink the image permanently.
- The layer:
  1. Pads to the diagonal size.
  2. Rotates on the padded canvas.
  3. Uses `_center_crop_to(rotated, orig_h, orig_w)` to center‑crop back to the original height/width.

So for an input of 1000×1000, the final output is also 1000×1000; only the padded border wedges are removed. Because of this, a separate `resize_to_original` flag is not necessary — the behavior is shape‑preserving and consistent with the existing `RandomRotation` API.

Happy to adjust anything if needed.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
@participant3 

> 3\. Applies a conservative center crop (`~1/sqrt(2)` of original H,W) that is guaranteed to remove all border/canvas artifacts for any rotation angle, while staying backend‑friendly and batched.
> 
> This is less aggressive than full angle‑dependent LRR math, but guarantees that the cropped region contains **no fill pixels**, which matches your "cropped out should not contain fill value" requirement.

I feel like this removes too much of the image, much more than it needs to for small angles (which is probably how this layer is used).

Can you add the math to compute the exact zoom factor needed for each angle so that cropping gives you exactly a rectangle that touches the original border of the image in 4 points while keeping the output size the same?
So for a square image for instance, as the angle increases from 0 to 45 degrees, the zoom factor increase from 1 to √2.
